d.title: Two graders, two positions in the graph, two different failures
d.caption: **The failure corrective RAG cannot see is the one where retrieval succeeded and generation still went wrong** — the right passage came back, the grader passed it, and the answer then asserted something the passage does not say. A document grader has no view of that, because when it runs there is no answer yet. **The two are siblings rather than alternatives**, and the honest default is the document grader first: bad retrieval is the commoner failure and chunks are cheaper to judge than a draft plus its context.

nodes.label: grade the DOCUMENTS
nodes.sub: corrective RAG - rewrite, retry, fall back

d.title: Four model calls for one answer, before any retry
d.caption: **That is the arithmetic to put in front of the decision.** A document grader plus a support check plus the generation plus the retry the support check triggers is four calls where the baseline was one — and the right question is whether an offline groundedness measurement already says the unsupported-claim rate is low enough to live with. **Measure before adding the second grader, not after.** And note the last row: a grader from the same model family shares the generator's blind spot, so the subtle overreach is exactly the case where both agree.

shares its blind spot - use another

d.title: Three conditions, and code generation is the only common task that meets them
d.caption: **Tree search multiplies where every pattern in the table adds.** A branching factor of three to depth four is up to 81 leaf trajectories, each a full agent run with its own tool calls, plus a value call at every node visited — the table's most expensive row is a rounding error against that. **So the three conditions are the decision**, and the third is the one that disqualifies most real systems: MCTS abandons a branch and resumes from an earlier state, which is impossible once an action has sent an email or charged a card.

d.title: Four questions a shared state schema never had to answer
d.caption: **Everything in section 05 assumed you own both ends.** Once the far agent belongs to another team, each row becomes a thing someone must invent and document — and A2A is one set of answers to exactly these four. **The task lifecycle is the choice that makes the rest fall out**, and `input-required` is the state most clients forget: a remote agent is allowed to stop and ask, which a function call has no way to express.

d.title: A capability you invoke, or a correspondent you delegate to
d.caption: **The two are described as competitors and are not.** A tool server has no goals: it offers functions, you call them, and it never comes back with a question. Another agent reasons, may refuse, may need something from you, and owns its own tools — which is why the unit of work has to be a task rather than a return value. **A system of any size uses both**, and the useful habit is asking which of these two things you are talking to before choosing the machinery.
